bridge: Builds on S06 least privilege, B04 boundaries and F05 credentials. No cloud account or paid resource is required for this policy exercise.
teaching:
Cloud shared responsibility divides duties between provider and customer according to the service. A managed database may remove host patching work while leaving customer identity, schema access and data-retention decisions. The boundary changes between infrastructure, platform and application services.

IAM evaluates principal, action, resource and conditions. A broad role can grant authority far beyond one app's needs. Prefer workload identities and scoped short-lived credentials where supported rather than embedding long-lived keys in source. Public browser configuration and a privileged server secret are different kinds of data.

Review effective policy, including inherited permissions and explicit-deny behaviour under the selected provider. Cloud terminology differs, so use its official evaluator rules. A policy's presence in a file is not proof it is attached to the deployed principal; verify the actual binding and test both permitted and forbidden operations.

A service name alone does not determine responsibility. For a cloud-hosted application, write a table of the data, accounts, application code, runtime, guest operating system, network controls and physical hosts, then identify who configures, patches, monitors and responds for each. A managed Kubernetes service can leave substantial cluster and workload responsibilities with the customer. Read the specific service’s current contract and documentation. Authentication establishes evidence about an identity; authorisation decides an operation on a resource. Federation and single sign-on reuse trust relationships but do not remove authorisation checks, token lifetimes or the need to revoke existing sessions.
example:
Provider-neutral teaching policy
Workload W may read bucket training-notes objects under prefix public/.
W may not write objects or read private/.
Assume this policy is the sole grant; default deny.
W read public/intro.txt -> allow
W read private/note.txt -> deny
W write public/new.txt -> deny
explanation: The sole-grant assumption makes the fixture determinate. A real account may inherit another grant, so effective access must include all applicable policy. A cloud access key copied into a frontend bundle would be visible to users; use only intentionally public client configuration there.
exercise: Evaluate the three supplied requests plus W deleting public/intro.txt. Then use this invented managed-database contract, not a real provider claim: provider patches physical hosts, host OS and database engine; customer manages users, data permissions and application code; provider performs scheduled backups only when customer enables/configures them; customer chooses retention and tests restore. Assign responsibility for data access, engine patching, backup configuration, backup execution and restore testing. No account or paid service is required.
solution: Read public/intro.txt allows; read private/note.txt, write public/new.txt and delete public/intro.txt all deny because the sole grant is read under public/. Under the invented contract, customer owns data-access policy, backup configuration/retention and restore testing; provider owns host/engine patching and execution of enabled scheduled backups. Execution and configuration are separate duties. For a real service, replace these assumptions with its current documented contract and deployed settings.
challenge: Design a least-privilege identity for a read-only report worker. State allowed resources/actions, credential lifetime, revocation/recovery and a negative permission test. Explain how you would verify the deployed binding.
challenge_solution: Example paper policy: report-worker may read only the designated report-input prefix and write only its output prefix if output storage is required; it cannot delete inputs or administer accounts. Prefer the platform’s scoped workload identity and short-lived credentials, with documented disable/revoke and job-recovery steps. Positive check reads an authorised synthetic input; negative checks deny another dataset and an input deletion. Inspect the actual deployed workload identity, role attachment and effective policy, then record observations from designated resources. A checked-in policy alone does not prove its deployment.
